operationalization: Score optical complexity (pigment, lens, aperture, resolution) across arthropods on an independent phylogeny and ask whether neighboring grades are each optically functional. A continuous series of useful grades would support the possibility of a selective path; a complex eye isolated from any functional intermediate, or intermediates that are optically useless, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D meshes of arthropod and vertebrate heads from which eye-region structure can be measured for a subset of taxa

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: opsin and eye-development gene sequences for comparing photoreceptor homology across grades

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic backbone on which eye grades can be mapped to test whether complexity changes in small steps

obstacles: Living grades are collateral relatives, not the ancestral sequence.
No public dataset scores optical performance across Articulata; those measurements are scattered in papers.
A functional series shows that intermediates are possible, not that selection produced any particular eye.
rationale: The comparative series Darwin appealed to can be approximated with phylogeny plus morphology, but eye-grade and optical-performance variables are not in one open table, so a team would spend months compiling them. Even a clean series would not reconstruct the historical path or separate selection from shared developmental constraint. Coverage is decent for insects and crustaceans and thin for the vertebrate extension of the scope.

operationalization: The sentence is a falsification rule: the theory fails if some complex organ could not possibly have been reached by successive slight modifications. No measurement records impossibility of every pathway, and a gap in known intermediates does not decide it.
obstacles: Impossibility of every gradual pathway is modal, not a dataset variable.
Missing intermediates are predicted both by true saltation and by an incomplete record, so the outcomes do not discriminate.
rationale: The empirical clause that no such organ is known reports a state of argument rather than a measurable frequency. Any organ still lacking a known intermediate is compatible with the rule, because the rule demands a demonstration of impossibility, which comparative and fossil data cannot supply. Scores stay near the floor because there is no decision criterion a dataset could meet.

operationalization: Code lung versus swim bladder, and flotation versus respiration, on a molecular vertebrate tree and reconstruct the ancestral state for lung-bearing vertebrates. The claim is supported if that ancestor is reconstructed as having a flotation swim bladder and lungs are derived from it; it is refuted if lungs (or a non-flotation air organ) are ancestral and swim bladders arise later inside ray-finned fishes.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: vertebrate phylogeny for ancestral-state reconstruction of air-filled organs

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences of early osteichthyans and sarcopterygians that bracket the relevant nodes

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: published morphological matrices that code respiratory and buoyancy structures in early vertebrates

obstacles: The flotation function and soft anatomy of the deep ancestor are rarely fossilized.
Coding lung and swim bladder as alternative states can smuggle in a homology decision.
Selection as the converting agent is not recorded by character order alone.
rationale: Public trees and morphological matrices make the direction of the transformation a standard ancestral-state problem, and that direction is the core of the historical claim. Soft-tissue function at the critical nodes is inferred rather than observed, so the flotation premise and the appeal to selection stay out of reach of the same datasets. The analysis is feasible for living osteichthyans and only a proxy for the unknown prototype.

operationalization: Map electric organs, and the tissues and genes that build them, onto a molecular fish tree. Independent origins from non-homologous muscle or nerve pathways confirm that similar organs need not be inherited from a common ancestor; a single origin with shared developmental identity would refute that reading for this case.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: genomes and ion-channel sequences of electric fishes used to test independent origins

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogeny of teleosts and cartilaginous fishes on which electric organs can be mapped

candidate_datasets.name: NCBI Gene Expression Omnibus
candidate_datasets.role: electric-organ versus muscle expression studies that show whether similar organs reuse the same inherited pathway

obstacles: Repeated origins show convergence more cleanly than they show that selection, rather than constraint, produced the similarity.
Luminous insects and the orchid–Asclepias cases are less completely sequenced than electric fishes.
rationale: The claim is existential: similar organs have sometimes been built independently. Electric fishes are the stated example, and public genomes, expression studies, and trees already contain the variables needed to separate convergence from homology. A small team can rerun that test in weeks. Other named cases are thinner, but they are not required to confirm or refute the 'sometimes' statement.

operationalization: Draw a sample of named organs across plants and animals and score whether a structurally intermediate form is known in a relative. The claim is supported if that fraction is high; it is weakened if a large share of organs, after a defined search, still lacks any intermediate.

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: character matrices that record intermediate states for particular organ systems in studied clades

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic context for deciding whether a similar structure in a relative counts as a transitional grade

obstacles: What counts as an organ or a transitional grade is not standardized.
Absence of a known grade is confounded by research effort and preservation.
No dataset enumerates organs across plants and animals.
rationale: Matrices exist for well-studied character systems, so a subset of organs can be scored, but the claim is a frequency across organs in general. Building that sampling frame would take years of literature coding, and failure to find a grade does not mean none exists. Discriminating power stays low because the result tracks the history of description as much as biology.

operationalization: Partition skeletal characters among mammals or birds into phylogenetic signal versus diet, habitat, and locomotion from trait databases. The claim is supported if most characters, including the shared limb skeleton, track clade membership rather than present habits; it is refuted if current ecology explains the chief part of structure.

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: species-level trees for mammals and birds used to measure phylogenetic signal

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: diet, foraging stratum, and body size as measures of present habits of life

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoSource
candidate_datasets.role: 3D limb and skeletal meshes for comparing homologous structure across divergent ecologies

obstacles: Phylogenetic signal can reflect constraint or low power rather than inheritance of unused structure.
Trait databases cover a small slice of 'the chief part of organisation', mostly vertebrates.
rationale: For the limb example and for bird and mammal ecology, open trees and trait tables support a standard comparative partition, and that analysis is weeks of work for a restricted scope. The claim is about most of the organization of every organism, which existing matrices do not cover. A correlation with current habits also would not prove that a trait arose for those habits, so the test is informative only for the mismatch Darwin named.

operationalization: For structures involved in interspecific interactions, compare fitness effects on the bearer and on the other species. One structure whose only effect is a benefit to another species, with no benefit to the bearer or its kin, would refute the claim; a survey that finds return benefits in candidate mutualisms supports it only weakly.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: catalog of interspecies interactions used to screen candidate structures, not to measure who benefits

obstacles: Interaction records do not contain fitness effects or exclusive beneficiaries.
Cryptic return benefits and parasite manipulation are hard to separate from a structure evolved for another species.
A universal negative cannot be confirmed by failing to find a case.
rationale: The refuting observation is well defined, but the variable that would show it, exclusive fitness benefit, is not a field in open interaction databases and is only scattered through experimental papers. GloBI can list mutualisms and antagonisms to examine, which is a partial screen. Coverage across all interacting species is negligible relative to the scope, and compilation would take far longer than weeks.

operationalization: Compare establishment and impact of species moved from larger biotas into smaller ones, including islands such as New Zealand, with the reverse direction. Systematic yielding of local endemics to invaders from richer biotas supports the biogeographic prediction; equal or reversed success would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: GloNAF
candidate_datasets.role: naturalized alien plants by region, including hundreds of islands, for comparing invasion into small versus large biotas

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrences of native and introduced taxa used to score establishment outside the native range

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: extinction risk and invasive-species threats for endemics after introductions

obstacles: Invasion success is confounded by propagule pressure, disturbance, and enemy release, not only relative perfection.
'As perfect as local competitors' is not itself a measured variable; establishment is a proxy.
GloNAF covers plants, while the claim is about inhabitants in general.
rationale: Open invasion and threat data can test the prediction that endemics of smaller regions yield to species from larger ones, and that analysis is standard. They do not measure degree of perfection or show that selection stopped at the local competitor. Discriminating power is limited by human-mediated confounds, so the result speaks to a restricted biogeographic proxy.

operationalization: On an amniote tree, date the origin of skull sutures relative to live birth and ask whether sutures are present in egg-laying relatives that do not use them in parturition. Origin of the trait before its mammalian use supports co-option in that example; a suture system that appears with live birth would count against it. 'Many modifications' would further require a frequency across traits.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: amniote phylogeny for ordering sutures against reproductive mode

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: matrices that code cranial sutures and reproductive characters in reptiles and mammals

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: dated trees for mammals and squamates used to place the origin of live birth

obstacles: Original lack of advantage is a historical negative that current non-use does not prove.
No catalog records which modifications began as non-adaptive byproducts.
Suture function during birth is not a field in trait databases.
rationale: The skull-suture example can be examined as a timing-of-function question with existing trees and matrices, but only after substantial interpretation of what 'laws of growth' and 'at first of no advantage' mean. The quantitative claim that many modifications follow this path has no dataset. Even a clear sequence would not separate later co-option from an earlier, undetected function.

operationalization: Measure morphological gaps between close relatives in well-sampled fossil clades and ask whether gaps shrink as specimens are added. Persistent large gaps after intense sampling would challenge a strict no-leap reading for those clades; gap-filling would support it only as a proxy, because the claim is about all past organisms, including those never preserved.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences through time for testing whether intermediates accumulate in densely sampled clades

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: morphological matrices for disparity and gap analyses along fossil phylogenies

obstacles: The claim is defined over all past organisms, most of which were never preserved, so residual gaps do not refute it.
Sampling and the Signor-Lipps effect manufacture apparent leaps.
'Strictly true' has no tolerance for a single saltation, which cannot be audited.
rationale: Fossil occurrences and character matrices can test a proxy, continuity in well-sampled clades, with standard disparity methods. The stated claim is insulated by whatever is missing from the record, so every remaining gap is compatible both with saltation and with incompleteness. That is why discriminating power is low even though the raw databases are strong.

operationalization: Within a class, compare a morphological distance matrix of fundamental structure with a molecular tree and with ecological similarity. Agreement with the molecular tree, and not with habits of life, supports unity of descent; grouping by habit rather than by independent genealogy would refute that explanation.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: class-level phylogenies synthesized largely from molecular studies, independent of the morphological types being explained

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequence data for rebuilding trees without using the structural characters under test

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: matrices of shared structure within classes for comparison with ecology and with molecular clades

obstacles: Some classes still have sparse morphological matrices or molecule-poor regions of the tree.
Particular characters can be conserved by constraint even when the nested body plan fits descent.
rationale: The explanatory claim has a direct comparative test: fundamental structure should track an independently estimated genealogy rather than way of life. Open trees, sequences, and morphological matrices cover the major classes well enough for that test, and using molecules avoids circularity with a morphology-based taxonomy. A small team can run the comparison with standard phylogenetic methods in weeks.

operationalization: For complex instincts with genetic data, compare heritability and response to selection on breeding values with transmission of acquired habit in cross-fostering or training designs. A predominant genetic component and negligible inheritance of learned habit would support the ranking; inheritance of trained behavior comparable to selection on spontaneous variants would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: genetic variants and behavioral phenotypes in Drosophila, a model for whether instinct-like behavior segregates genetically

candidate_datasets.name: Mouse Genome Informatics
candidate_datasets.role: alleles and phenotypes for innate behaviors such as burrowing, nest building, and parental care

obstacles: Public genetic data are concentrated in a few laboratory species, not animals in a state of nature.
Showing that a behavior is genetic does not show that selection accumulated it historically.
No dataset ranks the contribution of habit against selection across instincts.
rationale: Model-organism databases can reject a strong version of inherited habit for particular behaviors and can show genetic variation, which is part of the mechanism. They do not cover complex instincts in the wild, and they do not contain the selection history the claim puts first. The ranking 'chiefly' versus 'subordinate' therefore remains a proxy test on a small subset.

operationalization: For clades with a complex instinct, score behavioral intermediates on a phylogeny of related species. A graded series of collateral instincts supports the expectation; a complex instinct that appears in one step, with relatives lacking intermediate behavior after adequate study, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenies of insects, birds, and other groups in which behavioral grades would be ordered

candidate_datasets.name: AntWeb
candidate_datasets.role: species accounts that record colony behavior for a subset of ants

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: avian phylogeny for ordering nest-building and breeding behaviors among relatives

obstacles: Instinct scores are not a field in these databases and must be coded from natural-history literature.
Collateral grades are not ancestral stages.
Extinction of intermediate species removes the very evidence the prediction asks for.
rationale: Phylogenies are public and a few behavioral series, such as social insects and brood parasites, are described well enough to test gradation in those clades. There is no open ethogram database spanning complex instincts, so most of the scope would have to be compiled. Living intermediates also cannot show that the historical path was gradual rather than that side branches retained intermediate behavior.

operationalization: Among recorded interspecific behaviors, test whether any instinct increases another species' fitness while leaving the actor and its kin with no fitness gain. One such instinct would refute the claim; finding that apparent gifts, such as aphid honeydew or cleaner-fish service, return a benefit to the actor supports it only as a partial screen.

candidate_datasets.name: Global Biotic Interactions
candidate_datasets.role: interspecies interaction records, including mutualisms, used to list candidate behaviors

obstacles: GloBI does not encode instinct, exclusive benefit, or fitness.
Exploitation of another species' instinct is easily confused with an instinct performed for that species.
The universal wording cannot be confirmed by absence of a known case.
rationale: Interaction data can flag mutualisms and manipulations for follow-up, which is a restricted proxy for the universal negative. The decisive measurement, fitness to the actor versus fitness only to another species, is scattered through experiments and missing for nearly all interactions. Analysis at the stated scope is not a weeks-scale job on existing tables.

operationalization: Estimate within-species variance in migratory distance, direction, and propensity, and geographic variance in nest structure. Substantial variation, including populations that do not migrate, confirms the claim for the stated examples; invariant migration and invariant nest form across well-sampled species would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: individual tracking data for migratory direction, distance, and loss of migration

candidate_datasets.name: eBird
candidate_datasets.role: seasonal occurrence used to measure population differences in migratory extent

candidate_datasets.name: NestWatch
candidate_datasets.role: nest records for geographic variation in nest construction

obstacles: Tracked variation mixes innate differences with plasticity and condition.
Coverage is strong for birds, the named examples, and weaker for other wild animals.
rationale: The claim's own examples, migratory extent and direction and nest form, are variables in open tracking, occurrence, and nest datasets. A small team can quantify within-species variance with standard summaries in days to weeks. Plasticity means not every measured difference is an instinct in the strict sense, but the variation Darwin pointed to is directly observable and adequate for the bird-centered scope.

operationalization: Regress flight-initiation distance on island isolation, history of human presence, hunting pressure, and body size. Longer distances where persecution has been longer or more intense, and shorter distances on uninhabited islands, would support the claim; no such pattern, or a pattern explained by predator fauna alone, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Database of bird flight initiation distances
candidate_datasets.role: compiled alert and flight-initiation distances as a measure of fear of approaching humans

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: island versus continental distributions of the species in the flight-distance compilation

candidate_datasets.name: IUCN Red List
candidate_datasets.role: hunting and persecution coded among threats, as a proxy for exposure to humans

obstacles: Flight distance confounds evolved fear, individual learning, habitat, and the background predator community.
The compilations are snapshots, so they do not measure the word 'slowly'.
Geographic bias toward Europe, North America, and Australia leaves many persecution histories unsampled.
rationale: A large public compilation of approach distances makes the island-tameness and body-size contrasts testable for birds, together with range and threat data. That is a proxy for acquired fear, not a measurement of the rate of acquisition or of heritability. Confounds are serious enough that a positive correlation would remain ambiguous, and non-bird scope is barely covered.

operationalization: For breed-typical behaviors in dogs, chickens, pigeons, and rabbits, test whether alleles and selection scans account for the behavior, and whether trained habits are transmitted to untrained offspring. A genetic response to selection with no inheritance of training would support the selection half and weaken the habit half; the claim's 'both together' reading needs a quantitative split between the two.

candidate_datasets.name: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals
candidate_datasets.role: catalog of inherited behavioral and production traits in domestic species, with links to genes

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: breed genomes and variants used to look for selection on behavioral loci

obstacles: Inherited habit is not a variable in gene catalogs; those catalogs record genetic variants.
Pigeons and rabbits are much thinner than dogs and chickens.
Breed history confounds deliberate selection, drift, and training.
rationale: Open trait and genome resources can show that some domestic behaviors map to segregating variants, which speaks to selection on accidental differences. They do not measure the share due to inherited habit, which is half of the stated mechanism. The test is therefore informative for dogs and fowl and incomplete for the joint claim across the named domestic animals.

operationalization: Reconstruct nest-building versus facultative and obligate brood parasitism on a cuckoo phylogeny, and repeat for cowbirds and honeyguides. A derived obligate state with nesting or facultative ancestors supports the sequence; parasitism ancestral to the family, or no intermediate state where sampling is good, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic sample of cuckoos and other brood-parasitic birds for ancestral-state reconstruction

candidate_datasets.name: VertLife
candidate_datasets.role: alternative avian trees used to check that the reconstructed sequence is not an artifact of one phylogeny

obstacles: Parasitic status and nesting behavior are not columns in these tree repositories and must be coded from monographs.
The selective claim that fostered young fared better is not in phylogenetic presence-absence data.
Extinct intermediates and hosts leave no behavioral fossils.
rationale: The historical sequence is a standard ancestral-state question, and public bird trees cover cuckoos and the other parasitic groups well enough to try it. The behavioral coding step is literature compilation rather than a download, which holds data existence and feasibility at a moderate level. Even a clean sequence would not demonstrate the fitness advantage that is supposed to have driven the habit.

operationalization: Map predation on pupae, facultative slave-making, and obligate dulosis on an ant phylogeny focused on Formica and Polyergus. The claim is supported if dependent slave-makers are derived from raiders that still use foreign brood as food; it is weakened if dulosis is ancestral or arises without a predatory-raiding precursor.

candidate_datasets.name: AntWeb
candidate_datasets.role: species taxonomy and natural-history notes that identify dulotic ants and their hosts

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: formicine phylogeny for ordering food-raiding and slave-making

obstacles: Behavioral states are unevenly recorded and often absent for related species.
Collecting pupae as food is a historical function, not a preserved trait.
Territorial raiding is an alternative route to dulosis that phylogeny alone may not separate.
rationale: Ant taxonomy and trees are public, and the living grade from Formica to Polyergus is exactly the comparison Darwin used, so a partial phylogenetic test is realistic. Habit coding is incomplete outside the well-studied genera, and the original purpose of the raids is not a character in any database. The analysis would take months of literature harmonization rather than a short standard run.

operationalization: Order comb architecture, from irregular brood cells through intermediate stingless-bee combs to the hive-bee cell, on a corbiculate-bee phylogeny. A stepwise increase along the tree supports acquisition by successive modification; a phylogeny in which the architectural series is not a historical sequence, or a jump to hexagonal comb without intermediates, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogeny of bumblebees, stingless bees, and honeybees

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequences for corbiculate bees used to test relationships independently of nest architecture

obstacles: Quantitative nest-architecture scores are in papers, not in the sequence or tree databases.
A grade series of living bees can be ecological rather than the ancestral path.
Many stingless-bee nests are described qualitatively.
rationale: Relationships among the social bees Darwin arranged in a series are recoverable from public sequences and trees, so his particular order can be checked. The architectural measurements that would show slight successive modification are not in those databases. The test can support or upset the proposed sequence for this narrow clade and still leave the selective cause unmeasured.

operationalization: Compare observed cell angles, wall curvature, and bee spacing during construction with the geometry predicted by equal spheres whose intersections are built up. A match to those angles and to equal inter-bee distances would support the mechanism; systematic deviation, or construction kinematics that do not sweep spheres, would refute it.
obstacles: Cell measurements and construction videos are scattered in papers and are not a public comb database.
Wax rheology and local building rules can produce similar hexagons without bees sweeping equal spheres.
Finished-comb geometry does not record the positions bees occupied while building.
rationale: The geometric prediction is sharp enough to confirm or refute for Apis mellifera, whose comb has been measured many times. Those measurements are not gathered in an open dataset, so a reanalysis means compiling supplements and classic tables. Overlapping predictions from physical models of wax keep the test from cleanly isolating the behavioral story about equal spheres.

operationalization: Compute wax volume per unit of cell volume for real combs and for nearby alternative angles and wall thicknesses that bees could build. A match to the calculated minimum supports absolute economy; a feasible geometry that uses less wax refutes it.
obstacles: Empirical wall thicknesses and angles sit in scattered morphometric papers.
Economy of wax is not the only function; strength and brood packing define other optima.
'Could not lead further' depends on which construction constraints are treated as fixed.
rationale: The scope is a single well-measured object, the Apis comb, and the decision rule is a comparison with a calculated wax minimum, so the claim is operational. There is still no open morphometric database, which caps data existence, although a small team could recompute the comparison from published tables in weeks. Other functions of the comb mean a wax minimum need not be an architectural maximum.

operationalization: Test whether worker traits segregate in the parental genome and whether sterile castes evolve where within-colony relatedness is high. Parental transmission of worker phenotypes supports family-level selection; worker adaptations that cannot be transmitted by fertile parents, or that evolve where relatedness is too low for that pathway, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: social-insect genomes for asking whether worker traits have a heritable basis in reproductive individuals

candidate_datasets.name: AntWeb
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic distribution of sterile worker castes across ants

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogeny for comparative tests of caste evolution against relatedness and social system

obstacles: Colony relatedness estimates are scattered in papers, not in AntWeb or GenBank.
Haplodiploidy and manipulation hypotheses make similar predictions about sterile workers.
Termites and many wasps are poorly represented relative to honeybees and a few ant genera.
rationale: Genomes and caste lists make the genetic precondition of family selection testable in well-studied social insects. The relatedness and fitness data that would show selection on parents, rather than an alternative social mechanism, still have to be compiled. The scope includes all social insects with sterile castes, and public data match only a subset.

operationalization: Within single nests, test whether worker size and shape are continuously graded or fall into discrete modes, and estimate how often graded nests occur across species. Frequent within-nest gradations confirm the empirical clause; exclusively discrete castes with no graded species would refute the 'often' claim.

candidate_datasets.name: AntWeb
candidate_datasets.role: specimen images and morphometrics that can be grouped into colony series for polymorphic ants

obstacles: Many AntWeb specimens lack a same-nest identifier, so within-nest series must be filtered by hand.
Continuous variation can be nutrition rather than the selective gradation the theory invokes.
Bees, wasps, and termites are far less measured than ants.
rationale: Within-nest morphometrics are a direct test of the prediction that neuters in one nest sometimes grade into each other, and ant specimen data make a start. Colony context is incomplete, so adequacy and feasibility stay moderate, and the link from gradation to selection on parents is an extra inference. The frequency word 'often' needs a broader sample than the famous polymorphic genera.

operationalization: Code worker polymorphism as continuous, broadly graded, or discrete without intermediates, and reconstruct the sequence on an ant tree. Discrete castes derived from graded ancestors, as in driver ants relative to their relatives, would support the sequence; discrete castes arising without a graded precursor would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: AntWeb
candidate_datasets.role: morphometrics and images for scoring whether workers form a continuum or discrete castes

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: ant phylogeny for testing whether graded polymorphism precedes discrete castes

obstacles: Eliminating intermediates by selection is not distinguishable from a developmental switch using shape data alone.
Colony series and caste codes are missing for most species.
Driver ants are one clade; the scope is polymorphic ants generally.
rationale: The predicted order, graded series first and discrete extremes later, can be examined for ants with public specimens and a tree. That is a partial historical test. The selective elimination step is not in the morphometrics, and missing natural-history data keep the sample well short of all polymorphic ants. Harmonizing caste scores would take months.

operationalization: Compare behavioral similarity of sister species that live in distant regions with the ecological distance between those regions. High similarity of nest, migration, or foraging habits despite different conditions supports retention from a common ancestor; behavior tracking local conditions rather than relatedness would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: BirdTree
candidate_datasets.role: phylogeny for identifying closely allied bird species in distant regions

candidate_datasets.name: EltonTraits 1.0
candidate_datasets.role: foraging and diet traits as a limited proxy for retained habits

candidate_datasets.name: Movebank
candidate_datasets.role: migration tracks for comparing instinct-like movement among related species

obstacles: Foraging traits and tracks are proxies; nest, song, and display instincts are mostly uncoded.
Similar behavior can be shared selection in unmeasured niches rather than inheritance.
Thrushes and wrens illustrate a claim stated for allied animals generally.
rationale: Trees plus foraging and movement data can test a bird subset of retained habits under different geographies. That is narrower than instincts in general, and the datasets do not contain most of the behaviors Darwin had in mind. Similar habits also do not discriminate inheritance from parallel selection, so the explanatory half of the claim stays weakly tested.

operationalization: For species pairs, separate failure to produce offspring when parental gametogenesis is normal from sterility of F1 hybrids whose own gametogenesis fails. A systematic difference in the stage of failure supports two phenomena; a single shared stage of reproductive collapse would count against the distinction.

candidate_datasets.name: Drosophila speciation dataset
candidate_datasets.role: pairwise premating isolation and hybrid inviability or sterility scores that separate first-cross failure from hybrid sterility

obstacles: Outside Drosophila, crossing tables that record the stage of failure are scattered in papers.
The distinction is close to a definition by stage, so some of the result is built into the scoring.
Plants and non-fly animals in the stated scope are poorly represented in the open compilation.
rationale: One public compilation already splits barriers into components that match the two phenomena for many fly pairs, and that split can be reanalyzed quickly. The physiological claim is broader than Drosophila, and plant or vertebrate crosses with a recorded stage of failure are not in a comparable open table. Where the stage is scored directly, the contrast is informative rather than confounded.

operationalization: Regress fertility or offspring number on pedigree or genomic inbreeding coefficient, treating low inbreeding as the occasional cross with a less related mate. A negative slope confirms that closer interbreeding lowers fertility and that less related matings raise it; a flat or positive slope would refute the relationship.

candidate_datasets.name: Song sparrow pedigree and fitness
candidate_datasets.role: individual inbreeding coefficients and lifetime offspring counts in a wild bird population

candidate_datasets.name: Soay sheep inbreeding and fitness
candidate_datasets.role: pedigree and genomic inbreeding with annual breeding success in a free-living mammal

candidate_datasets.name: Mouse Genome Informatics
candidate_datasets.role: reproductive phenotypes of inbred mouse strains as an extreme of close interbreeding

obstacles: These open pedigrees are animals; plant inbreeding-depression tables are more scattered.
The further application to hybrids kept for several generations is not the design of these wild pedigrees.
Environmental stress changes the slope, so a single population is not the whole relationship.
rationale: Fertility and inbreeding coefficient are measured together in more than one public pedigree, and the decision rule is a standard regression that a small team can run quickly. The same negative relationship is widely tabulated for other animals and for plants, so the stated generality is not hanging on one species. What the datasets do not settle is Darwin's use of the pattern to explain multi-generation hybrid decline in particular.

operationalization: Compare intrinsic hybrid sterility between the wild progenitors of a domestic animal with fertility among the domestic descendants supposed to combine those progenitors. Loss of a barrier that is still present in the wild pair would support removal by domestication; barriers that are unchanged, or domestic forms that never had intersterile progenitors, would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Online Mendelian Inheritance in Animals
candidate_datasets.role: fertility and reproductive-disorder records for domestic breeds

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: genomes used to test whether dogs, cattle, and similar domestics actually descend from more than one species

obstacles: Fertility of the original wild crosses at the time of domestication is rarely measured.
Several of the multi-species origin stories are themselves uncertain, which confounds the comparison.
Selection on fertility under domestication is hard to separate from hybrid ancestry.
rationale: Genomes can check the historical premise that particular domestics combine more than one species, and breed databases record present fertility. The variable that would show sterility being removed, a before-and-after barrier between the same lineages, is mostly absent. The test therefore covers a few candidate domestics and does not reach the general mechanism.

operationalization: Estimate the proportion of interspecific crosses with reduced fertility of the first cross or the hybrids, and ask whether any well-documented crosses are fully fertile. A high proportion plus at least some fully fertile exceptions would support 'extremely general but not universal'; either rarity of sterility or no fertile exceptions would count against that wording.

candidate_datasets.name: Drosophila speciation dataset
candidate_datasets.role: quantitative isolation scores for a large set of species pairs inside one genus

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: divergence times used to restrict the proportion to pairs that are genuine species rather than populations

obstacles: Published crosses favor tractable taxa and both unusually fertile and unusually sterile outcomes.
Drosophila does not stand in for plants and animals at large.
Taxonomic rank affects the denominator of 'between species'.
rationale: The frequency claim has an obvious proportion, and one open dataset can estimate it inside Drosophila, including pairs fertile enough to challenge universality. Sampling bias and narrow taxonomy keep that from being a test of plants and animals generally. A broader compilation exists only as papers and would take months to harmonize.

operationalization: Correlate an index of how hard a first cross is to make with the sterility of the resulting hybrids, across species pairs. A positive but noisy association, with many pairs off the line, supports a loose correspondence; a tight relationship or no relationship would refute the stated pattern.

candidate_datasets.name: Drosophila speciation dataset
candidate_datasets.role: paired premating or crossing difficulty and postzygotic sterility for the same species pairs

obstacles: The open numerical compilation is essentially Drosophila.
Ascertainment favors pairs that someone managed to cross.
Premating scores are an imperfect stand-in for Darwin's 'difficulty of making a first cross'.
rationale: Where both variables were scored on the same pairs, the loose-correspondence claim is a straightforward correlation with a clear null of either a strict line or no association. That test is feasible now for flies and is discriminating within that genus. It remains a restricted-scope test of a claim stated for plants and animals, because comparable paired tables elsewhere are not in one open file.

operationalization: Regress first-cross success and hybrid fertility on genetic or phylogenetic distance. A strong positive relationship of isolation with distance, with residual scatter and with no hybrids between families, supports affinity as a large but not strict governor; no relationship, or frequent fertile crosses between distant families, would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Drosophila speciation dataset
candidate_datasets.role: isolation indices paired with genetic distance for fly species

candidate_datasets.name: TimeTree
candidate_datasets.role: divergence times as an independent measure of systematic affinity outside the fly compilation

candidate_datasets.name: GenBank
candidate_datasets.role: sequences for estimating genetic distance of additional crossed pairs without using fertility to define affinity

obstacles: Crossing outcomes outside a few model clades are not in the same table as the distances.
Family rank is a human cutoff, so 'never between families' partly reflects how families were drawn.
Genetic distance is a proxy for the systematic affinity of 1859 classifications.
rationale: Genetic distance is a better independent measure of affinity than a taxonomy that may already have used fertility, and the fly dataset plus public distances make the regression a standard analysis. Discriminating power is high inside the clades that have both variables. Adequacy is only partial because plants, vertebrates, and most invertebrates lack a similarly complete open crossing table.

operationalization: For species pairs crossed in both directions, compare offspring production with the sexes reversed. Frequent large asymmetries support the claim; consistently equal reciprocal success would refute the statement that the difference is often very wide.

candidate_datasets.name: Drosophila speciation dataset
candidate_datasets.role: isolation scores that incorporate reciprocal crosses, though many published indices collapse the two directions

obstacles: Major compilations often average or sum reciprocal outcomes, erasing the contrast.
Direction-specific tables for plants, Fucus, and vertebrates are scattered.
A difference in success does not by itself locate the cause in an imperceptible reproductive detail.
rationale: The comparison of reciprocal directions is simple and highly discriminating when both directions were published separately. The most convenient open fly compilation often folds those directions into one index, so recovering the asymmetry means going back to papers. That is a feasible partial test, not a ready analysis of plants and animals at the stated scope.

operationalization: Compare postzygotic sterility in sympatric and allopatric pairs after accounting for genetic distance. Sterility that tracks divergence in allopatry, where it could not have been endowed to prevent crossing, supports an incidental byproduct; sterility concentrated only where species meet, beyond what distance predicts, would favor a special isolating endowment.

candidate_datasets.name: Drosophila speciation dataset
candidate_datasets.role: postzygotic isolation, genetic distance, and range overlap for sympatric versus allopatric pairs

candidate_datasets.name: GBIF
candidate_datasets.role: occurrence ranges for scoring overlap of additional species pairs

obstacles: The rival hypothesis of reinforcement applies more clearly to premating barriers than to sterility.
'Unknown differences in the reproductive system' is not itself a measured variable.
Range-overlap scores in the fly table do not extend to the full scope of crossable species.
rationale: The anti-teleological claim can be turned into a geographic prediction, and an open fly dataset already contains isolation, distance, and overlap. That is informative but not decisive, because incidental divergence and several selection scenarios can produce the same distance relationship. The vague residue, unknown differences chiefly in the reproductive system, is not an additional dataset test.

operationalization: Among first crosses that fail, record the fraction in which fertilization occurs and the embryo dies early, versus no fertilization or death at a later stage. A large share of early embryonic death would support 'very frequent'; a minority share would refute that wording.

candidate_datasets.name: Drosophila speciation dataset
candidate_datasets.role: hybrid inviability scores that mark offspring death without separating embryonic from later stages

obstacles: Most isolation indices do not record the developmental stage of death.
Gallinaceous birds and plants, the groups Darwin emphasized, lack a public stage-of-failure table.
Crosses that produce no visible embryo are easily misclassified.
rationale: The frequency of early embryo death is a clear proportion, but open compilations usually score inviability without the stage. Stage-resolved cases exist in papers on a few birds, plants, and model animals, which is enough for a partial look and not enough for the stated generality. Building the denominator would be slow literature work.

operationalization: Compare, across taxa, whether captivity and hybridization both impair gametogenesis while leaving general health intact. A shared pattern restricted to the reproductive system would support the resemblance; sterility in captivity that tracks nutrition, behavior, or whole-body illness, unlike hybrid incompatibilities, would weaken it.
obstacles: Zoo and studbook records that would measure captive sterility are not openly downloadable.
Hybrid and captivity studies rarely use the same taxa and the same health measures.
Resemblance of outcomes does not show resemblance of causes.
rationale: The parallel is testable in principle with matched measures of gonad function and general health, and fragments of both literatures exist. No public dataset lines up captive sterility with hybrid sterility, so data existence stays low and a harmonized analysis would be slow. Even a matched pattern would be confounded by the many unrelated ways captivity reduces breeding.

operationalization: Plot fitness against environmental distance from the parental environment, and offspring fitness against parental genetic or phenotypic distance. A benefit at slight distances and sterility or reduced vigor at large distances would support both clauses; monotonic harm from any change, or no heterosis at slight genetic distance, would count against the corresponding clause.

candidate_datasets.name: Song sparrow pedigree and fitness
candidate_datasets.role: fitness across a range of parental relatedness, a test of the slight-cross half rather than of changed conditions

obstacles: Environmental-distance experiments and crossing experiments are different datasets and are rarely paired.
'All organic beings' is far broader than any public reaction-norm table.
Slight versus great is an undefined cutoff.
rationale: Each half can be proxied, heterosis with pedigrees and beneficial acclimation with transplant experiments, but they are not one analysis and the environmental half is scattered. The joint hump-shaped claim is only partly operational until 'slight' is given a scale. Existing open fitness pedigrees cover animals far better than the full scope.

operationalization: Compare the distribution of cross-fertility among named varieties with that among named species. Overlap, including partly sterile variety crosses such as maize lines, supports the denial of a universal fertility of varieties and of a fundamental fertility criterion; completely non-overlapping distributions would refute that denial.

candidate_datasets.name: MaizeGDB
candidate_datasets.role: maize stocks, crosses, and fertility-related traits among domesticated lines that rank as varieties

candidate_datasets.name: Drosophila speciation dataset
candidate_datasets.role: interspecific fertility scores used as the species side of the comparison

obstacles: Varieties have often been ranked as varieties because they interbreed, which circularizes the contrast.
Maize and flies do not represent natural and domestic varieties generally.
Partial sterility in crops can be chromosomal engineering rather than the spontaneous case Darwin cited.
rationale: Overlap between variety-cross fertility and species-cross fertility is a direct test of the denial that fertility draws a fundamental line, and both kinds of scores exist in public resources for particular groups. Circularity in how taxonomists applied the ranks is a real confound, though genetic clusters can be defined without using fertility. The sample is a subset of the stated scope and would need months to broaden.

operationalization: Compare phenotypic variance of F1 hybrids with variance in F2 and later generations, and inspect marker segregation. Much greater later-generation variance confirms the pattern; equal variance refutes it. Segregation of intact parental alleles refutes a disturbed reproductive system as the cause, whereas chaotic gamete failure would support that cause.

candidate_datasets.name: MaizeGDB
candidate_datasets.role: mapping populations and phenotypes for comparing first-generation and later-generation hybrid variance

candidate_datasets.name: 1001 Genomes
candidate_datasets.role: Arabidopsis accessions and recombinant populations with genotypes that show whether later-generation variation is Mendelian

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: Drosophila cross and phenotype records for F1 uniformity versus later segregation

obstacles: Mapping populations are richer for crops and model animals than for arbitrary hybrids.
Later-generation variance also rises because of recombination even when fertility is normal, which is the alternative cause.
rationale: Public mapping populations record both phenotypes across hybrid generations and markers that identify the cause of the extra variance. The pattern Darwin reported is therefore decidable, and the disturbed-reproduction explanation can be separated from ordinary segregation. Coverage is a subset of all hybrids but includes both plants and animals at a scale a small team can analyze with standard quantitative genetics.

operationalization: Holding fertility aside, compare interspecific hybrids and intraspecific mongrels on variance, dominance or prepotency, reversion rate, and parent-offspring resemblance. Similar distributions support the claim; a large, repeatable difference on any of those properties would count against a general close similarity.

candidate_datasets.name: MaizeGDB
candidate_datasets.role: phenotypes of crosses among maize lines and with wild relatives, spanning variety and species distances

candidate_datasets.name: FlyBase
candidate_datasets.role: cross records for within-species and between-species Drosophila progeny

obstacles: Prepotency and reversion are not standardized fields.
Species and variety crosses are rarely measured with the same traits in the same experiment.
Similarity is a judgment across several phenomena, each of which could differ.
rationale: A few model systems have both kinds of cross and could be compared on variance and resemblance, which is a partial test. The open databases do not code prepotency or reversion, so those parts of the list still sit in narrative breeding records. Matched designs are uncommon, and feasibility is closer to months of harmonization than to a ready analysis.

operationalization: Whether species and varieties differ fundamentally is a judgment about taxonomic rank and about what would count as a fundamental difference. Overlap in fertility or genetics can be measured, but that overlap does not decide the philosophical conclusion, and rank itself is partly defined by the same facts.
obstacles: 'Fundamental distinction' has no measurement that would settle it.
Tests that use the labels species and variety inherit the criteria used to apply those labels.
The hybridism facts are evidence in an argument, not a separate empirical outcome.
rationale: Neighboring claims about fertility distributions are empirical; this sentence is the conceptual summary that those facts support no fundamental distinction. Any dataset result can be redescribed as a difference of degree or of kind depending on the species concept adopted. Because the rivals are not separated by a measurable consequence beyond that definitional choice, the claim is not empirically resolvable.

operationalization: In well-fossilized clades, place fossils and reconstructed ancestors in morphospace relative to living species pairs. Ancestors and fossils that lie off the straight line between two living species, and that connect each species to an earlier node, support the prediction; a surplus of fossils that are direct morphological intermediates between living species would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences and ages for locating extinct forms relative to living species

candidate_datasets.name: MorphoBank
candidate_datasets.role: character matrices for measuring whether fossils fall between living species or on stems

candidate_datasets.name: Open Tree of Life
candidate_datasets.role: phylogenetic placement of living species whose last common ancestor is being compared

obstacles: Multidimensional morphology makes 'directly intermediate' ambiguous.
Only clades with dense fossils and coded characters can be used.
Unequal rates of change move ancestors off the midpoint even when the path was a direct bridge.
rationale: Occurrences, matrices, and trees are public and sufficient for a geometric test in a minority of clades. That is a restricted-scope proxy for a claim about all related species, most of which lack fossils. Discriminating power is moderate because off-midpoint ancestors are also produced by rate variation, not only by the branching structure Darwin described.

operationalization: Estimate cumulative species numbers through time from fossil occurrences and phylogenies and compare them with living richness and with described fossil species. A total vastly larger than the known record is consistent with the rhetoric; a reconstructed history with only modestly more links than living species would challenge it. No numerical cutoff defines 'inconceivably great'.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil taxon counts and ranges used to estimate past diversity and the size of the unsampled remainder

candidate_datasets.name: Catalogue of Life
candidate_datasets.role: living species totals as the denominator for how many links gradual connection would require

obstacles: 'Inconceivably great' has no refuting threshold.
The number is largely a deduction from gradual steps plus deep time, so the test is partly circular.
Preservation bias dominates any estimate of true past diversity.
rationale: Public inventories can support order-of-magnitude diversity estimates, which is why data existence is fairly high, but the claim does not state a number that those estimates could miss. Because the result is entailed by gradualism once time is long, a large estimate does little to separate this sentence from its premise. This was one of the harder items to score because the rhetorical quantifier resists a decision rule.

operationalization: Compare Darwin's figure of about 300 million years since the latter part of the Secondary period with the radiometric age of the Chalk and of Weald denudation. An elapsed time of that order would support the inference; an age several times shorter would refute it. Measured coastal-retreat rates can separately check the one-inch-per-century premise.

candidate_datasets.name: International Commission on Stratigraphy
candidate_datasets.role: geologic time scale giving radiometric ages for the late Cretaceous Chalk and the Cenozoic

candidate_datasets.name: British Geological Survey
candidate_datasets.role: maps and memoirs of the Weald used to identify the rocks and the denudation being dated

obstacles: Modern cliff retreat varies by lithology and setting, so the erosion-rate premise is noisier than the age of the Chalk.
Which bed counts as the latter part of the Secondary period shifts the target age by tens of millions of years, not by the factor at issue.
rationale: The claim is a specific duration for a named English denudation and for time since the late Chalk. The international time scale and British geological mapping contain those ages at the needed resolution, and comparing them with 300 million years is immediate. Radiometric ages do not depend on the denudation-rate assumption, so the elapsed-time conclusion can be confirmed or refuted cleanly.

operationalization: Compare the fossil record of wholly soft-bodied living phyla with that of biomineralizing taxa, and compare shell and bone preservation with sedimentation rate and depth. Any well-documented soft-bodied fossil refutes the absolute bar on preservation; a large deficit of soft-bodied taxa, and loss of shells where sediment does not accumulate, supports the bias claim.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil occurrences by taxon and preservation, including soft-bodied lagerstätten

candidate_datasets.name: Ocean Biodiversity Information System
candidate_datasets.role: living marine occurrences used as the denominator of which soft-bodied groups could have been preserved

candidate_datasets.name: World Register of Marine Species
candidate_datasets.role: taxonomic list of soft-bodied versus mineralized marine organisms

obstacles: Exceptional preservation and secondary mineral films mean 'wholly soft' is not a single taphonomic class.
Deep-sea living faunas and non-depositional seafloors are still unevenly sampled.
rationale: Open fossil and living-marine databases contain the taxa, preservation modes, and environments needed to test both the absolute wording and the bias. A small team can cross-tabulate soft-bodied groups against fossil occurrences with standard joins. The absolute claim and the bias claim can come apart, and that split is itself a decisive outcome rather than a confound that blocks the test.

operationalization: Measure hiatus lengths between successive fossiliferous formations and compare them with the durations of the formations themselves. Gaps as long as or longer than the recorded intervals support wide unrecorded separations; continuously recorded succession would count against that pattern. Ranking gaps as the chief cause requires comparing their contribution with other biases.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: stratigraphic columns with unit ages and gaps between packages

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil collections tied to units, to restrict the comparison to fossiliferous formations

obstacles: Macrostrat coverage is much denser in some continents than worldwide.
Calling gaps the chief cause requires a model that partitions incompleteness among erosion, non-deposition, facies, and collection bias.
Unconformities can be brief locally and still look wide in a compiled column.
rationale: Gap durations are a native variable of open stratigraphic databases, and computing them against formation durations is a standard analysis a small team can do quickly. That settles whether separations are wide over a large part of the sedimentary record. It does not by itself show that those gaps, rather than the other biases Darwin listed, are the main source of imperfection, which is why the verdict stays partial.

operationalization: Relate formation thickness and fossil richness in shallow-marine units to independent evidence of subsidence, such as tectonic setting and backstripping, not to thickness alone. A positive association during slow subsidence with sediment keeping pace would support the claim; thick fossil-rich sections formed mainly during uplift or non-depositional deepening would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: unit thickness, lithology, and environment for ancient sedimentary formations

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: fossil richness of those units

obstacles: Thickness is often used to infer subsidence, which makes the association partly circular.
Independent tectonic evidence is uneven outside well-studied basins.
The wording 'all our ancient formations' is stronger than any basin sample.
rationale: Thickness, environment, and fossil counts are downloadable and can be joined, so the association is testable in studied basins within weeks to a few months. Circularity between thickness and inferred subsidence is the main limit on discriminating power. The result would cover a large marine sample and still fall short of every ancient fossiliferous formation.

operationalization: Compare per-capita origination and extinction of shallow-marine genera between intervals independently classed as regional uplift and as subsidence, and ask whether fossil-rich rock is concentrated in the subsidence bins. Higher origination during elevation and higher extinction plus richer deposits during subsidence would support the coupling; the reverse pattern would refute it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: genus first and last appearances and collection counts through time

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: packaging of fossil-bearing rock against relative sea level and accommodation

obstacles: The amount of preserved rock covaries with sea level, so apparent speciation and extinction track sampling.
Varieties and coastal faunas are poorly resolved compared with marine shelly genera.
Uplift intervals are exactly when the record is worst, so the predicted speciation peak is hardest to see.
rationale: Origination, extinction, and the stratigraphic context of fossil-rich rock are all in public databases, and the correlation has a standard form. Sampling bias that moves with sea level is severe enough that the same pattern is predicted without any change in true speciation, so discriminating power stays limited. The test also substitutes marine genera for the varieties and coastal species in the claim.

operationalization: Compare the duration of individual formations with observed species durations and with molecular estimates of time to speciation. Formations systematically shorter than speciation times would support the claim and the expectation that one formation rarely holds a full graded series; formation durations as long as species transformations would count against it.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: first and last appearances used as observed species durations

candidate_datasets.name: Macrostrat
candidate_datasets.role: ages and thicknesses of formations whose durations are being compared

candidate_datasets.name: International Commission on Stratigraphy
candidate_datasets.role: radiometric ages that convert formation boundaries into durations

obstacles: Observed species durations are truncated and extended by sampling, so they are a biased clock for speciation.
A formation can be short and still capture a rapid local transition.
Molecular speciation intervals and fossil durations measure different things.
rationale: Formation ages and taxon ranges are public, and the comparison of their durations is feasible with ordinary database queries. Both clocks are distorted by the same incomplete record, so a numerical inequality is only a partial test of whether one formation should contain a graded species series. Adequacy is good in well-dated marine basins and poor for most terrestrial formations.

operationalization: For marine species whose first local occurrence is above the base of a formation, test whether older occurrences exist in other regions. A majority with earlier records elsewhere would support immigration as the usual explanation; a majority with no earlier record anywhere, in well-sampled groups, would favor local origin.

candidate_datasets.name: Paleobiology Database
candidate_datasets.role: geographic and stratigraphic occurrences used to compare local first appearances with earlier records elsewhere

obstacles: Failure to find an older record elsewhere is weak evidence of in-situ origin because most regions are undersampled.
Many species are known from a single basin, so the test has no second locality.
Reworking and uncertain correlation can create false earlier occurrences.
rationale: The immigration test is a spatial query on a single open occurrence database and is practical to run. It can confirm immigration whenever an older external record exists, which is the informative direction. The converse, local origin, is hardly distinguishable from incomplete geographic sampling, so the claim that immigration is the usual explanation stays only partly decidable.
